content: Between 6% and 15% of newborns develop hyperbilirubinemia that requires medical intervention. Effective management of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia depends on both prevention and early treatment, with phototherapy being the primary treatment method. Oral zinc has been suggested as a potential intervention to lower serum total bilirubin (STB) levels, possibly by reducing enterohepatic circulation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of oral zinc supplementation, compared to placebo or no treatment, on the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia in neonates during their first week of life. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the safety profile of oral zinc in these infants. The researchers conducted a systematic search of CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library 2014, Issue 1), MEDLINE (1966 to November 30, 2014), and EMBASE (1990 to November 30, 2014). Randomized controlled trials were included if they involved neonates (both term and preterm) who received oral zinc at a dose of 10 to 20 mg/day within the first 96 hours of life, for any duration up to day seven, compared to no treatment or placebo. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for this review. In this study, oral zinc was administered at a dose of 5 mL twice daily from day 2 to day 7 postpartum. The zinc was given directly into the infant's mouth using a plastic measuring device provided with the bottle or a spoon. The incidence of hyperbilirubinemia, defined as STB levels ≥ 15 mg/dL, was found to be similar between the zinc and placebo groups (286 participants; risk ratio [RR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58 to 1.52). The mean STB levels at 72 ± 12 hours were also comparable between the two groups (286 participants; mean difference [MD] -0.20, 95% CI -1.03 to 0.63). Although the duration of phototherapy was significantly shorter in the zinc group compared to the placebo group (286 participants; MD -12.80 hours, 95% CI -16.93 to -8.67), the overall incidence of requiring phototherapy was similar between the two groups (286 participants; RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.66 to 2.18). Adverse effects such as vomiting (286 participants; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.25), diarrhea (286 participants; RR 2.92, 95% CI 0.31 to 27.71), and rash (286 participants; RR 2.92, 95% CI 0.12 to 71.03) were rare and did not differ significantly between the groups. In conclusion, the limited evidence available does not support the use of oral zinc supplementation in neonates up to one week old as a means to reduce the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia or the need for phototherapy.
